parts.title: Opinion Matching - Test 02
parts.instructions: Read the four texts. For each statement, choose the person (Person A, Person B, Person C, or Person D) who expresses that opinion.
parts.topic: Four people respond to the interview on their attitude toward art. Read their interviews and answer the questions below.

people.name: Person A
people.biographyText: I know the names of some famous artists, and I recognize some paintings. However, I only go to exhibitions when my friends want to. I find that seeing exhibitions is often boring, and while I appreciate the skill it takes to create art, I can't help but feel that many galleries lack excitement. Despite this, I do have some artistic techniques myself; I enjoy painting in my free time but I prefer to create rather than just observe.

people.name: Person B
people.biographyText: I think that looking at art is a personal experience. I much prefer to see art on my own, where I can take my time to appreciate each piece without distractions. I think visitors to galleries should focus more on the art itself rather than chatting or using their phones. When I'm alone with a painting, I can truly connect with it and reflect on what the artist intended.

people.name: Person C
people.biographyText: I find art fascinating. I have developed a good knowledge about various art movements and techniques over the years. Each piece tells a story, and I love discovering the history behind them. The colors, forms, and emotions captured in art pieces captivate my imagination. I could spend hours discussing and analyzing art, and I always look forward to learning more.

people.name: Person D
people.biographyText: I have great memories associated with art, as I have been going to numerous art exhibitions in my whole life. I cherish the moments spent with friends and family, exploring galleries together. Seeing art with people close to me adds a special dimension to the experience; we share our thoughts and feelings about the pieces we encounter. These shared experiences have created lasting bonds and wonderful memories.

parts.title: Matching Headings - Test 02
parts.instructions: Read the passage quickly. Choose a heading for each numbered paragraph (1-7) from the drop-down box.

paragraphs.text: The growing discussion around a four-day working week suggests that the traditional five-day schedule is losing its appeal. Many companies still rely on outdated, industrial-age patterns, believing long hours guarantee higher performance. However, today's employees are no longer satisfied with this rigid approach. They increasingly value balance, flexibility, and personal wellbeing over mere presence at the office. In many cases, long working hours bring stress and exhaustion rather than productivity. As a result, the old system is slowly becoming less relevant to modern life.

A shorter working week offers employees clear and meaningful advantages. The standard five-day routine leaves little time for family, health, or leisure, which often leads to fatigue. For women in particular, the challenge is greater, since many carry responsibility for both work and household duties. An extra day off allows people to recharge and focus on personal needs, making them happier and more balanced. This balance can then increase motivation and commitment in the workplace. In the long term, such benefits may raise overall productivity.

Many business owners argue that fewer working hours will inevitably reduce profit. Evidence from real cases shows that these concerns cannot be ignored. In the UK, one company trialled the policy and reported a 30% drop in output. Similarly, in one city, the change caused losses of around 30 million dollars in just one month. These examples make many employers reluctant to introduce the system on a wide scale.

The shorter week may also create unexpected difficulties for employees. Although some firms report that work is still completed on time, this often comes at a cost. Compressing tasks into fewer hours can increase mistakes and raise stress levels. Workers sometimes take projects home, which defeats the purpose of having more free time. Over time, this added pressure can reduce rather than improve wellbeing. Therefore, the model may not be as sustainable as it first appears.

Changing long-established working habits is another major obstacle to adopting a four-day working week. For decades, both employers and employees have become accustomed to the traditional five-day schedule, making it difficult to accept a new routine. Many managers still believe that spending more time in the office reflects greater commitment and productivity, even when evidence suggests otherwise. Employees may also worry that working fewer days could affect their career opportunities or income. As a result, resistance to change remains strong, slowing down the widespread adoption of the four-day working model.

While a shorter working week may seem attractive, it does not benefit everyone equally. Employees in education, healthcare, and emergency services cannot simply reduce their hours without harming those who depend on them. Similarly, small businesses may lack the resources to reorganize schedules or hire extra staff. As a result, the policy risks creating inequality: office workers may enjoy more free time, while others are forced to continue with long and exhausting shifts. If fairness is not addressed, the four-day week could deepen divisions between different sectors of society.

Instead of focusing only on reducing the number of working days, other reforms may bring broader and fairer results. Flexible hours, remote work opportunities, or job-sharing can give employees greater control over their routines without cutting productivity. Companies can also invest in better training, digital tools, and mental health support to improve efficiency and wellbeing. By adopting a mix of strategies, employers may create healthier workplaces that serve both business needs and individual lives. In this way, balance and satisfaction can be achieved without the risks tied to a strict four-day model.
